name: quickjs
why: A tiny embeddable JavaScript engine by Fabrice Bellard, compact and impressive to explore though JS is familiar.

brief.what_it_is: QuickJS is a small, embeddable JavaScript engine written in C, supporting the ES2025 specification. It takes JavaScript source and runs it through an interpreter via the command-line tool qjs, or can compile JavaScript into standalone executables with qjsc. The homepage says it has no external dependencies and a small built-in standard library with C library wrappers.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage pitches it as a small, easily embeddable engine with very low startup time, for use where a full JavaScript runtime is too heavy. It is by Fabrice Bellard, with copyright shared with Charlie Gordon.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes a fast interpreter and garbage collection by reference counting, with cycle removal, which the author says reduces memory use and gives deterministic behavior. The command-line interpreter's contextual colorization is implemented in JavaScript. The project also embeds the libregexp, libunicode and dtoa C libraries, which can be reused separately.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no build steps beyond the downloads. Options listed: a source tarball (quickjs-2026-06-04.tar.xz), an extras tarball with Unicode tables and the bench-v8 benchmark, the official GitHub repository, binary releases, and a Cosmopolitan build (quickjs-cosmo-2026-06-04.zip) that the author says runs on Linux, Mac, Windows, FreeBSD, OpenBSD and NetBSD on ARM64 and x86_64. The brew formula installs the qjs and qjsc executables.
brief.standout: It is tiny for a spec-complete engine: the author cites 367 KiB of x86 code for a hello world program and a runtime lifecycle under 300 microseconds. It also compiles JavaScript into standalone executables with no external dependency, and the TypeScript and Babel compilers have been built to run on it.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage news lists releases on 2025-04-26, 2025-09-13 and 2026-06-04, the latest with a changelog and a claim of 42% speedup over the previous release on bench-v8. The homepage itself was reachable and current.
brief.caveats: The 2025-04-26 release removed the bignum extensions and the qjscalc application, so anyone looking for qjscalc should use the BFCalc web calculator the homepage links to instead. Performance and conformance figures (nearly 100% of test262 for ES2025, 42% faster) are the author's own claims, not independently verified here. The homepage does not give a build walkthrough for the source tarball. The Micro QuickJS microcontroller variant is only mentioned as a link, not described.
quotes: Small and easily embeddable: just a few C files, no external dependency, 367 KiB of x86 code for a simple hello world program.
Garbage collection using reference counting (to reduce memory usage and have deterministic behavior) with cycle removal.
The complete life cycle of a runtime instance completes in less than 300 microseconds.
fetch_log: https://bellard.org/quickjs/ - fetched successfully; homepage text includes news, features, downloads, documentation and licensing. Documentation, GitHub and demo links were named but their URLs were not shown in the returned text, so they were not followed.

judge.reason: A tiny, embeddable, spec-complete JavaScript engine that can compile scripts into standalone executables makes runtime internals unusually approachable and surprising.

entry.title: QuickJS
entry.tldr: A complete JavaScript engine in a few C files, small enough to embed anywhere, that can also compile scripts into standalone executables.
entry.deeper_look:
QuickJS is a JavaScript engine written in C by Fabrice Bellard, with copyright shared with Charlie Gordon. It targets the ES2025 specification. The `qjs` command runs JavaScript through an interpreter, and `qjsc` compiles a script into a standalone executable with no external dependencies.

It exists for places where a full JavaScript runtime is too heavy. The homepage pitches it as small and easily embeddable, with very low startup time. It cites 367 KiB of x86 code for a hello world program and a full runtime lifecycle under 300 microseconds. Those figures are the author's own.

The interesting idea is how little a spec-complete language implementation needs. Memory is managed by reference counting with cycle removal, which the author says keeps memory use down and makes behavior deterministic. The interpreter's contextual colorization is written in JavaScript. The regex, Unicode and dtoa pieces (libregexp, libunicode, dtoa) are separate C libraries that can be reused on their own. The author also reports that the TypeScript and Babel compilers have been built to run on it.

It is a good project to read as well as run. The engine is compact enough that you can plausibly follow how a modern JavaScript implementation fits together.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the interpreter's options, including how to run a script, evaluate an expression, or start the interactive REPL.
Shows how to compile a JavaScript file into a standalone executable or C output.

entry.whats_unique: It is a nearly complete modern JavaScript engine that stays tiny, and it can turn scripts into self-contained binaries. Its regex, Unicode and number-formatting libraries can be lifted out and reused separately.
entry.caveats: The 2025-04-26 release removed the bignum extensions and the qjscalc app, and the speed and conformance figures are the author's own claims.
